summary: Boundary value problem with exactly one solution.

methods.name: General solution, then boundary conditions
methods.reason: The equation is linear, so its general solution has two constants for the two conditions to determine.

steps.title: Write the characteristic equation
steps.text: For constant coefficients, try \(y = e^{rx}\). Substituting and dividing by \(e^{rx}\) leaves a quadratic in \(r\).

steps.title: Solve for the roots
steps.text: The discriminant is negative, so the roots are complex, \(r = \alpha \pm \beta i\). They give \(e^{\alpha x}\cos \beta x\) and \(e^{\alpha x}\sin \beta x\).

steps.title: Write the general solution
steps.text: Combine the two independent solutions with arbitrary constants.

steps.title: General solution
steps.text: Found by: characteristic equation. A boundary value problem fixes the solution at two different points, instead of fixing \(y\) and \(y'\) at one point. Unlike an initial value problem it can have exactly one solution, none, or infinitely many.

steps.title: Impose the boundary conditions
steps.text: Each condition gives one linear equation for \(C_1\) and \(C_2\).

steps.title: Solve for the constants
steps.text: The two equations are independent, so there is exactly one solution.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: This problem has exactly one solution.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Checked by substituting back into the equation, and it meets both boundary conditions.

methods.verify_note: Checked by substituting back into the equation, and it meets both boundary conditions.
